title: Elementary Idea of Valence Bond Theory
topicTitle: Elementary idea of Valence Bond Theory
notes: **Valence Bond Theory (VBT):** Proposed by Heitler and London (1927) and extended by Pauling and Slater, VBT states that a covalent bond forms when two atoms approach closely enough for their half-filled atomic orbitals to overlap. The electrons in the overlapping orbitals must have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle), and the system lowers its potential energy as the nuclei are attracted to the shared electron pair.

**Overlap condition:** The strength of a covalent bond is directly proportional to the extent of orbital overlap. Greater overlap means greater electron density between the nuclei and a stronger, shorter bond. This is why s–s overlap (e.g., H₂) is particularly effective — spherical s orbitals can achieve maximum head-on overlap along the internuclear axis.

**Sigma ($\sigma$) bond:** Formed by the end-to-end (axial) overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis. Any type of orbital can participate: s–s, s–p, or p–p (head-on). Once a $\sigma$ bond forms between two atoms, free rotation about the bond axis is possible because the electron density is cylindrically symmetric. Examples: H–H in H₂ ($1s–1s$ overlap), H–Cl in HCl ($1s–3p_z$ overlap).

**Pi ($\pi$) bond:** Formed by the sideways (lateral) overlap of two parallel p-orbitals. The electron density is concentrated above and below the internuclear plane, with a nodal plane containing the nuclei. Because rotation would destroy the parallel alignment of the p-orbitals, $\pi$ bonds restrict rotation — this is the origin of cis/trans isomerism in alkenes. Example: the second bond in C₂H₄ (one $\sigma$ + one $\pi$).

**Bond strength order:** $\sigma > \pi$ because end-on overlap is greater than sideways overlap. A typical C–C $\sigma$ bond has a bond energy of ~347 kJ/mol, while a C=C $\pi$ bond adds only ~265 kJ/mol (not double a $\sigma$ bond). This difference explains why $\pi$ bonds are more reactive — they are easier to break in addition reactions.

**Completely filled orbitals do not form bonds:** According to VBT, both overlapping orbitals must contain at least one unpaired electron. Two fully filled orbitals cannot form a covalent bond (they would violate the Pauli exclusion principle if the electrons tried to pair). This explains why noble gases are inert.

**Directionality of covalent bonds:** Covalent bonds are highly directional because maximum overlap occurs only in specific orientations. This contrasts with ionic bonds, which are non-directional (electrostatic attraction acts equally in all directions). The directionality of covalent bonds determines molecular geometry.

**Bond formation as an energy minimum:** When two H atoms approach, the attractive force (nucleus-electron) initially dominates, lowering the potential energy. At a certain internuclear distance (the bond length, 74 pm for H₂), the attractive and repulsive forces balance — this is the point of minimum energy. If the atoms move closer, nuclear-nuclear and electron-electron repulsions dominate sharply, raising the energy.

**Molecular orbital picture within VBT:** VBT treats the bond as a localized overlap between two atoms, unlike MO theory which delocalizes electrons over the whole molecule. VBT successfully explains the bonding in simple molecules like H₂, He₂⁺ (bond order 0.5), and HF, but struggles with molecules like O₂ (paramagnetism) and benzene (resonance).

**Electronic configuration prerequisite:** For VBT to predict bonding correctly, atoms must have unpaired electrons in their valence shell. For example, carbon in its ground state ($1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p_x^1\, 2p_y^1$) has only two unpaired electrons and should form only two bonds — yet it forms four. This paradox is resolved by invoking hybridization (next topic).

**Heitler–London treatment of H₂:** The first successful quantum mechanical description of a chemical bond. The wave function for H₂ is approximated as $\Psi = \psi_A(1)\psi_B(2) + \psi_A(2)\psi_B(1)$, representing the two electrons being shared between atoms A and B. This symmetric spatial function combines with an antisymmetric spin function (singlet state) to give a bonding interaction.

**Covalent bond types by overlap:** (i) s–s: H₂, (ii) s–p: HCl, HF, (iii) p–p ($\sigma$): Cl₂, F₂, (iv) p–p ($\pi$): the $\pi$ component of C=C, C≡C, (v) sp–sp: H–C≡C–H (ethyne sigma framework). Each type has characteristic bond lengths and strengths.

**Resonance in VBT:** When a single Lewis structure cannot represent a molecule (e.g., ozone O₃, benzene C₆H₆), VBT uses the concept of resonance — the actual structure is a hybrid of multiple contributing structures. The resonance hybrid is more stable than any single contributor (resonance stabilization energy).

**Limitations of VBT:** (1) Cannot explain the paramagnetism of O₂ (requires MO theory), (2) Does not account for delocalized bonding in aromatic systems without ad-hoc resonance, (3) Does not predict magnetic properties, (4) Fails for molecules with electron deficiency (e.g., B₂H₆). Despite this, VBT remains essential for understanding bond formation qualitatively.

**Real-world relevance:** VBT underpins the understanding of organic reaction mechanisms — nucleophilic substitution involves the overlap of a nucleophile's lone pair with an antibonding orbital, and electrophilic addition to alkenes involves the $\pi$ bond acting as an electron source. Understanding $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonding is critical for predicting reactivity in organic synthesis.
confusion: Sigma vs. Pi bond strength: Students often think a double bond is exactly twice as strong as a single bond. In fact, a C=C double bond (~614 kJ/mol) is weaker than twice a C–C single bond (~694 kJ/mol) because the $\pi$ component is weaker than the $\sigma$ component. The $\pi$ bond breaks first in addition reactions.

Orbital overlap does not require identical orbitals: A bond between 1s(H) and 3p(Cl) in HCl is perfectly valid despite the size mismatch. VBT only requires that the orbitals have compatible symmetry and sufficient energy overlap — not that they be the same type.

Hybridization is a mathematical construct, not a physical process: Orbitals do not literally 'mix' — hybridization is a way to construct a better approximate wave function that matches observed molecular geometries. The atom's electrons occupy hybrid orbitals in the bonded state, but this is a model, not a literal rearrangement.

Filled orbitals cannot share electrons to form a bond: Two atoms each bringing a filled orbital (e.g., two He atoms) cannot form a stable bond because all four electrons would have to occupy the same region with paired spins, violating the Pauli exclusion principle. This is why He₂ does not exist.

Pi bonds require parallel p-orbitals, not just any two p-orbitals: For a $\pi$ bond to form, the two p-orbitals must be parallel to each other and perpendicular to the internuclear axis. If they are perpendicular to each other (e.g., pₓ on one atom and pᵧ on the other), no effective sideways overlap occurs.
practice: Draw the orbital overlap diagram for HCl, showing the 1s orbital of hydrogen overlapping with the 3pᵧ orbital of chlorine along the internuclear axis. Label the bond as $\sigma$ and indicate the phase (+/−) of each lobe.
For the ethene molecule (C₂H₄), identify all the sigma and pi bonds. State which atomic orbitals overlap to form each bond, and explain why rotation about the C=C bond is restricted.
Calculate the bond order of He₂⁺ using the molecular orbital approach and explain, using VBT concepts, why He₂⁺ is stable while He₂ is not. (Hint: He₂⁺ has 3 electrons; the bond order is 0.5.)

Explain why N₂ has a triple bond consisting of one $\sigma$ and two $\pi$ bonds, while O₂ has a double bond. Use electronic configurations (N: $1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p^3$; O: $1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p^4$) to justify the number of unpaired electrons available for bonding.

Benzene (C₆H₆) has a planar hexagonal structure. Describe the bonding in terms of VBT: identify the $\sigma$ framework (sp² hybridization) and explain how the six p-orbitals overlap sideways to form a delocalized $\pi$ system. Why does this make benzene unusually stable?
universalFacts: VBT was the first quantum mechanical theory of the covalent bond and earned Linus Pauling the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. His book 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond' remains a foundational text.
The bond length of H₂ (74 pm) is one of the shortest covalent bonds because hydrogen's 1s orbital is very small and can achieve extremely close approach between nuclei.

All single bonds are sigma bonds. Double bonds consist of one sigma + one pi bond. Triple bonds consist of one sigma + two pi bonds. This pattern holds for all homonuclear and heteronuclear diatomic and polyatomic molecules.
The paramagnetism of liquid oxygen (it is attracted to a magnetic field) was one of the key observations that VBT could not explain, directly motivating the development of Molecular Orbital Theory.

Van't Hoff and Le Bel (1874) proposed that carbon's four bonds point toward the corners of a tetrahedron — a geometric insight that predated quantum mechanics and later found its explanation through sp³ hybridization in VBT.
